nameStory: Rock Shingle Lichen gets its name from its distinctive growth pattern that resembles overlapping wooden shingles on a roof. The flat, scale-like lobes layer over each other as they spread across rock surfaces, creating that familiar shingled appearance that anyone who's seen old New England architecture would recognize instantly.
description: Rock Shingle Lichen is a foliose (leaf-like) lichen that forms distinctive overlapping patches on rocks, looking remarkably like tiny gray-green roof shingles. Each individual lobe is flat and scale-like, typically measuring just a few millimeters across, but colonies can spread to cover several inches of rock surface. The overall color ranges from pale gray to greenish-gray, often with darker edges that give each 'shingle' a subtle outline.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms overlapping, shingle-like lobes that feel papery-thin and somewhat brittle when dry, becoming more pliable when moist

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale gray to greenish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet, with darker margins along each lobe

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on hard rock surfaces, particularly granite and other acidic rocks in exposed locations

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth to slightly rough, like fine sandpaper, while the underside is typically white to pale with simple attachment points

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are small (2-5mm), but colonies can spread across hand-sized areas or larger on suitable rock faces

habitat: Rock Shingle Lichen thrives on exposed granite outcrops, cliff faces, and large boulders throughout New England's mountainous regions. It prefers acidic rock surfaces in areas with good air circulation and moderate moisture, often found at higher elevations where fog and clean air provide ideal growing conditions.

seasonality.spring: Colors become more vibrant green with spring rains and increased humidity. Growth activity begins as temperatures warm, though changes are barely perceptible.
seasonality.summer: Appears more gray and contracted during dry spells, but shows beautiful green coloration after summer thunderstorms. Most active growing period despite appearing dormant.
seasonality.fall: Responds well to increased moisture from fall rains, showing good color contrast between wet and dry periods as weather becomes more variable.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow and ice, appearing quite gray and dormant but actually continuing slow metabolic processes during warm winter days.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare in New England with only one recorded observation, Rock Shingle Lichen can live for centuries, growing so slowly that a colony the size of your palm might be older than the oldest trees in the forest around it.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, gray foliose lichens on rocks, but the distinctive overlapping shingle pattern is unique - think of how you'd arrange playing cards in a fan, but flattened against the rock surface.
contextualKnowledge: Rock Shingle Lichen belongs to a small, specialized family (Vahliellaceae) that was only recently recognized as distinct from other lichen families, highlighting how much we're still learning about these remarkable organisms.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus recorded in New England, Rock Shingle Lichen is most easily compared to other small, gray rock lichens like those in the Lecidea group. However, its distinctive overlapping, shingle-like growth form sets it apart from the more typical flat or slightly raised patches of most rock-dwelling lichens.
